explainedBy: A retail trader sits at his workstation staring in shock at a stock chart that has plummeted 50%.

storyboard.claim: A stock chart collapses by 50% on the trader's screen.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail trader at a dual-monitor workstation looks worriedly at a crashed stock line.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opening scene establishing the trader confronting a market collapse.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the viewer in the trader's seat witnessing the severe 50% drop.

explainedBy: The seated trader rationalizes the bleeding red chart as an irresistible cheap bargain.

storyboard.claim: The trader's brain misinterprets a collapsing stock as a bargain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The seated trader smiles and talks at his screen, treating the red drop as an opportunity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the trader at the desk as his cognitive bias takes over.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the objective market collapse with the trader's naive optimism.

explainedBy: The trader looks over at a second screen where another stock has blasted through its all-time high.

storyboard.claim: A second stock blasts through its all-time high into uncharted territory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The trader points in astonishment at a second monitor showing a vertical breakout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the plunged stock on screen one with an explosive breakout on screen two.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the stark divergence between the two charts confronting the trader.

explainedBy: The trader recoils in fear from the high-flying stock, convincing himself it is too expensive.

storyboard.claim: The trader's fear instincts label the breakout stock as too expensive and terrifying.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The trader slumps in his chair with a fearful expression, backing away from the breakout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the psychological flip side of fear preventing buying at highs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the emotional dread of feeling you missed the boat.

explainedBy: The trader rationalizes that the high stock must crash, falling into the ultimate psychological trap.

storyboard.claim: Believing cheap stocks must bounce and expensive stocks must crash is a recurring psychological trap.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The trader at his desk speaks with concern, caught in the documented retail trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the twin cognitive biases as a historical psychological trap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the dual instincts as the primary driver of retail trading failure.

explainedBy: Almost all retail investors inevitably click buy on the cheap, falling stock.

storyboard.claim: 98% of retail investors click buy on falling, supposedly cheap stocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail trader clicks his screen to purchase the falling stock.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the trap springing as retail traders execute the wrong decision.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the overwhelming 98% statistical majority making this mistake.

explainedBy: The retail investor sits helplessly watching his stock slowly bleed out and collapse to zero.

storyboard.claim: Retail investors watch helplessly as their cheap stock collapses toward zero.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The trader slumps at his workstation watching the crash icon as his position dissolves.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The catastrophic outcome of buying the falling stock.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the emotional defeat of bag-holding a dying position.

explainedBy: Institutional fund managers aggressively buy the expensive stock at all-time highs, fueling a massive breakout.

storyboard.claim: Institutional funds aggressively buy stocks at all-time highs, pushing them into vertical breakouts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A confident institutional manager in a navy suit points decisively at market breakout feeds.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts from retail defeat to institutional dominance on the opposite trade.
storyboard.addedInformation: Demonstrates why institutional volume drives the real winners higher.

explainedBy: An investor clutches his money worriedly, questioning why natural human instincts betray traders under pressure.

storyboard.claim: Natural human psychology is wired to fail when real financial capital is at stake.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor stands holding a coin with an anxious expression, reflecting on his losses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the market divergence to the underlying psychological cause.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grounds the existential question in the physical preservation of capital.

explainedBy: A spectrum contrasts human instincts: the retail fear of heights on the left against the craving for bargains on the right.

storyboard.claim: Human instincts swing between fear of high prices and the irrational craving for cheap bargains.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum diagram plotting the emotional tension between fear of heights and desire for bargains.
storyboard.onScreenText: FEAR OF HEIGHTS / DESIRE FOR A BARGAIN
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Breaks down the psychological instincts named in the previous beat into measurable poles.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the dual emotional biases governing retail behavior without sound.

explainedBy: An investor slumps at his workstation as his emotional attachment to corporate stories destroys his portfolio.

storyboard.claim: The emotional need to be right about a story is what destroys investor portfolios.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps at his trading desk looking distraught as his capital deteriorates.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the emotional trap by showing the final damage to capital.
storyboard.addedInformation: Pinpoints the root cause of ruin: ego and narrative attachment.

explainedBy: The investor holds up William J. O'Neil's landmark study as the hosts introduce the deep dive.

storyboard.claim: The episode unpacks William J. O'Neil's exhaustive historical market study.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An investor in a study room holds the research book introducing O'Neil's masterwork.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the authoritative source material that solves the retail dilemma.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the foundation of empirical historical research.

callout.text: HOW TO MAKE MONEY IN STOCKS

explainedBy: The investor presents the classic book How to Make Money in Stocks to decode the CAN SLIM system.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil's research was codified in the book How to Make Money in Stocks and the CAN SLIM system.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor continues holding the book, smiling as the title and mission are highlighted.
storyboard.onScreenText: HOW TO MAKE MONEY IN STOCKS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects O'Neil's monumental research to the published book title.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clearly names the book and the CAN SLIM system under investigation.

explainedBy: A refute diagram rejects the assumption that O'Neil's work is a traditional guide of memorized ratios.

storyboard.claim: This work is not a traditional stock-picking guide or a list of financial ratios.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A refute diagram crosses out the traditional stock guide model on the cue phrase.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Dismantles the conventional view of financial investing guides.
storyboard.addedInformation: Forces a fundamental reframe before exploring the actual rules.

explainedBy: The investor points to the core reframe: an uncompromising psychological framework for an unfeeling market.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil's system is an uncompromising psychological framework for operating in an unfeeling market.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor stands in an abstract analytical space emphasizing psychological discipline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides the correct replacement model after refuting the traditional ratio myth.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the true nature of market mastery as psychological rigor.

explainedBy: An institutional manager indicates the balance of supply and demand governed by institutional volume.

storyboard.claim: The market is governed entirely by supply, demand, and institutional footprints.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager points at a balance scale icon representing supply and demand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the mechanical forces driving stock price movements.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes supply and demand visible as the objective balance of market forces.

explainedBy: A retail investor slumps with worry, confronting the reality that personal opinions and brand attachments are deadly.

storyboard.claim: Personal opinions and brand attachments are irrelevant and deadly to portfolio returns.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A retail investor slumps at his workstation acknowledging the fatal flaw of opinion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts institutional market mechanics with retail emotional attachment.
storyboard.addedInformation: Warns viewers against falling in love with company products or narratives.

explainedBy: The trader discusses value hunting, which historical data mathematically proves to be a losing game.

storyboard.claim: Value hunting for cheap overlooked stocks is mathematically proven to be a losing retail game.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The seated trader speaks with dismay at his workstation about the failure of value hunting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Tackles and rejects the popular myth of retail value investing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes the mathematical certainty of underperformance in cheap stocks.

explainedBy: The investor points in an analytical space, establishing disciplined pattern recognition as the only true edge.

storyboard.claim: The only edge for survival and success is disciplined pattern recognition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points to chart patterns in an analytical space, focusing on disciplined recognition.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from failing strategies to the trader's only proven edge.
storyboard.addedInformation: Focuses the visual on precision pattern identification.

explainedBy: The investor holds a protective shield representing strict mathematical risk control rather than guesswork.

storyboard.claim: Survival requires strict mathematical risk control rather than guessing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor holds a shield in an abstract analytical set, symbolizing capital protection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pairs pattern recognition with defensive risk management.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reinforces defense and rule-based risk mitigation as non-negotiable.

explainedBy: The investor in his study examines historical notes spanning 125 years of stock market winners.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil analyzed the greatest market winners across 125 years of history.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor holds research notes beside a clock icon, impressed by the historical scope.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands on the empirical depth of O'Neil's research.
storyboard.addedInformation: Illustrates the massive 125-year timescale behind the study.

explainedBy: A timeline spectrum displays the full data range stretching from the 1880s to 2008.

storyboard.claim: The historical dataset stretches from the 1880s all the way to 2008.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum diagram anchoring the 1880s on the left and 2008 on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the 125-year timeline concrete with specific boundary dates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Demonstrates the immense empirical span tested across market cycles.

explainedBy: An institutional analyst points out the comparison between an 1885 railroad and 21st century tech leaders Apple and Google.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil compared 19th-century railroads directly with modern leaders like Apple and Google.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager points at modern market charts comparing historical and modern titans.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides concrete historical and contemporary examples from the dataset.
storyboard.addedInformation: Juxtaposes disparate eras to highlight the boldness of the comparative study.

explainedBy: The investor examines historical market data with a magnifier, uncovering the shared DNA of over 1,000 super winners.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil decoded the exact common traits shared by over 1,000 super winners before their massive runs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor inspects records with a magnifier beside a trophy icon representing super winners.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the key output of the 125-year study: the shared precursor DNA.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the rigorous forensic analysis of top-performing stocks.

explainedBy: The retail investor asks why studying an 1880s railroad matters when the modern technological world is completely different.

storyboard.claim: Skeptics question how an 1880s railroad can provide insight into modern tech companies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail trader talks with an inquisitive, doubtful look at his workstation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Voices the intuitive skepticism of modern investors.
storyboard.addedInformation: Articulates the core objection regarding changing technology.

explainedBy: The institutional manager explains to the investor that while technology changes, human nature and supply and demand never change.

storyboard.claim: Human nature and the fundamental law of supply and demand remain unchanged across market eras.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional fund manager speaks authoritatively beside the balance icon to the listening retail trader.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the skepticism by identifying the unchanging constant: human psychology and supply/demand.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames market pricing as an unchanging reflection of human behavior.

explainedBy: A matchWave diagram synchronizes panic and greed across 1901 ticker tapes and 2001 digital screens.

storyboard.claim: Market panic and greed look identical on a 1901 ticker tape and a 2001 digital screen.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A matchWave diagram showing the synchronized emotional waveforms of panic and greed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Demonstrates the exact visual equivalence of market psychology across a century.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the identical emotional cycles visible as matching waves.

explainedBy: The investor holds the book beside a target icon, celebrating the codified seven-trait CAN SLIM formula.

storyboard.claim: The 125-year study codified the seven-trait CAN SLIM formula for identifying super winners.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor smiles holding the research book next to a target icon symbolizing CAN SLIM criteria.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Synthesizes the historical findings into the codified seven-trait formula.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the CAN SLIM acronym as the distillation of historical winners.

explainedBy: A flow diagram maps the foundation of CAN SLIM leading into the fundamental earnings engine.

storyboard.claim: The C and A components form the foundational engine of the CAN SLIM framework.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram showing the progression from foundation to fundamental engine.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins unpacking the specific letters of CAN SLIM, starting with C and A.
storyboard.addedInformation: Structures the mechanics visually as an engine.

explainedBy: The institutional manager emphasizes quarterly earnings acceleration and annual growth as non-negotiable standards.

storyboard.claim: Current quarterly earnings acceleration and annual growth are mandatory requirements for any stock.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An institutional manager explains the strict earnings standard on the trading floor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines what C and A stand for in practical company performance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes earnings acceleration as the non-negotiable baseline filter.

explainedBy: A CEO stands at the head of a mahogany table in a tense corporate boardroom.

storyboard.claim: Imagine a tense corporate boardroom with the CEO standing at the head of the table.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An executive in a tailored suit stands at the head of the conference room table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the narrative parable illustrating corporate earnings announcements.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the corporate boardroom setting for the earnings drama.

explainedBy: The CEO taps a laser pointer on his presentation slide, projecting confidence despite pressure.

storyboard.claim: The CEO projects complete confidence while tapping his presentation slide.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The CEO smirks and points firmly toward his presentation screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the boardroom scene as the CEO prepares to announce results.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts the corporate theater used to sell quarterly performance.

explainedBy: The CEO proudly announces a 12% quarterly earnings gain to a room of nodding executives.

storyboard.claim: The CEO proudly announces a 12% quarterly earnings gain to his nodding board.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The CEO speaks happily to the executives, announcing the 12% figure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The CEO delivers the climactic announcement of the 12% number.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the 12% figure that conventional executives celebrate.

explainedBy: While the corporate board claps in celebration, a disciplined investor sits quietly in the back evaluating the number.

storyboard.claim: The board applauds steady earnings, but an O'Neil investor sits unmoved in the back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits calmly in the background while the executive in front celebrates.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the board's conventional applause with the disciplined investor's skepticism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the dramatic clash of perspectives within the same room.

explainedBy: The investor takes the beautifully printed quarterly report and discards it in the trash.

storyboard.claim: The investor quietly takes the quarterly report, crumples it, and throws it away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor reaches out and takes the quarterly financial report to toss it out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The investor takes physical action rejecting the mediocre 12% report.
storyboard.addedInformation: Executes the vivid deed of taking the glossy report before discarding it.

explainedBy: The investor holds the crumpled report, rejecting 12% as a rounding error and demanding 50%.

storyboard.claim: In the stock market, 12% is a rounding error; super winners require 50% earnings growth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor holds the crumpled report with a sharp smirk, demanding explosive 50% growth.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Articulates why the report was discarded: 12% is completely insufficient.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the high quantitative threshold required by CAN SLIM.

explainedBy: An institutional manager explains that mediocre 10 to 12% earnings growth is a massive liability.

storyboard.claim: Mediocre 10-12% earnings growth is a massive liability that fails to attract institutional money.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional fund manager talks candidly about fund requirements on the trading floor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the institutional mechanics behind rejecting 12% gains.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes 'steady' corporate earnings as dangerous investment mediocrity.

explainedBy: The manager points out that small earnings increases cannot generate the frantic institutional buying needed to double a stock.

storyboard.claim: Small gains cannot generate the massive institutional buying needed to double or triple a stock.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager points emphatically at the trading floor volume displays.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the chapter on why only explosive earnings spark institutional accumulation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the transition to the required 25-50% baseline in the next beat.
